# Velocity matching for robot-object control (2026-03-18 20:00Z)

_**User**_

this is a section from my methodology "
\subsubsection{Robot-Object System Control}

The goal of the control system is twofold: to maintain the AFC configuration $C^\star$, and to move the object toward the desired waypoints produced by the planning algorithm.
Implementation differs according to robot kinematics.
As discussed in the Background (Section~\ref{sec:robots_dynamics}), for sticking contact the robot must achieve the exact velocity of the contact point corresponding to the desired object motion, given by the kinematic constraint \eqref{eq:background_velocity_at_point} \cite{lit review, manymore, MotionCone}.

If the robots are \emph{holonomic}, the problem is a velocity-tracking task: the velocity setpoint is obtained from a simple P-control comparing the current object state to the desired state, and can be realized using feedback such as motor encoders.
If the robots are \emph{non-holonomic} (e.g., differential drive), the desired contact-point velocity may not be feasible for a single robot; in that case, feasibility is addressed in the planning phase (e.g., by choosing waypoints and contact assignments so that the required contact velocities lie within the robot's motion constraints).

We can reduce the complexity of the robot-object dynamics by exploiting \emph{quasi-static}, also referred to as \emph{differential flatness} in this context \cite{pushing_revisited}.
When the object velocity is constant over a short time interval, the resulting trajectory is well-defined and admits a dual mapping between trajectory and velocity: the trajectory can be recovered from the flat output (e.g., the motion of a point related to the center of rotation), and vice versa.
For our object under AFC, such a segment is either a straight line or an arc \cite{pushing_revisited}.
The same observation holds for a differential-drive or Ackermann robot under constant velocity: the path is again composed of straight segments and arcs.
Therefore, if we represent the collision-free trajectory as a sequence of arcs and lines, there is a direct mapping from the object motion to the robot motion at each segment, provided the robot heading and the contact point on the robot are chosen appropriately.
This mapping is enforced at the velocity level by equating the object-side and robot-side contact velocities:
\begin{equation}
  \boldsymbol{v}_{\mathrm{contact}}
  \;=\;
  \zobjectvelocity
  \;+\;
  \zvelotheta \,\boldsymbol{k} \times \boldsymbol{r}_{\mathrm{com\text{-}to\text{-}contact}}
  \;=\;
  R(\zeta)
  \begin{bmatrix}
    v_r \\[2pt] 0
  \end{bmatrix}
  + \omega_r \times \boldsymbol{r}_{\mathrm{base\text{-}to\text{-}contact}},
\end{equation}
where the left-hand side reproduces \eqref{eq:background_velocity_at_point} and, for a differential-drive robot, $v_r$ and $\omega_r$ are the linear and angular velocities induced by the wheel speeds, mapped through the robot kinematics.

Concretely, this mapping amounts to finding two degrees of freedom per robot: the \emph{heading} $\zeta$ of the robot and the \emph{intended contact position} on the robot body, such that the contact-point velocity from the object side (given by \eqref{eq:background_velocity_at_point}) matches the contact-point velocity that the robot can produce at that body point.
A brief argument for existence: because the object pose has three degrees of freedom (position and orientation in $\zse$) while each robot contributes at least two (e.g., position of a point on the robot and its heading), the system is redundant; the mapping from the ``larger'' object motion to the ``smaller'' robot motion is underdetermined, so a solution that satisfies the contact velocity constraint can typically be found by suitable choice of robot heading and contact location.
This concludes our proposed method for configuration maintenance and object motion control.

So the three trajectories are the object's center-of-mass and contact point, the holonomic robot's trajectory matching that contact point, and the differential-drive robot's trajectory also matching it. I should plot all three together to demonstrate they align at the contact point.

For the visualization, I'm thinking a main figure showing the object outline at start and end positions, the center-of-mass path, contact point trajectory with normal vectors, and both robot trajectories overlaid. Then separate detailed figures for the holonomic and differential-drive cases showing robot poses at sample times with velocity vectors at the contact point to verify they match.

Actually, the user wants something simpler to demonstrate the concept rather than publication-quality plots. I should scale back to just one or two figures with a few subplots instead.

One important thing to verify for the holonomic case—I need to show that the matching works for different contact point locations around the robot body, not just a single α value. And for the differential-drive robot, I should check that the determinant stays non-zero to ensure the solution is valid.

I'll set up the script with command-line arguments for flexibility, using sensible defaults so the user can easily test different configurations without modifying the code.</details></think>

{
  "plan": "# Velocity Matching Test Script\n\nTarget file: [&#96;scripts/test/basic_test/test_matchingvelo.py&#96;](scripts/test/basic_test/test_matchingvelo.py)\n\n## Key Idea\n\nGiven an object under constant body-frame velocity &#96;(vx_b, vy_b, omega)&#96;, its CoM traces a straight line (omega=0) or an arc (omega!=0). A chosen contact point on the object boundary traces its own curve with a known velocity at every instant. We show that a circular robot can always produce this same contact-point velocity, for both holonomic and non-holonomic (diff-drive) kinematics, by choosing the right heading and contact position on the robot body.\n\n## Dependencies / Imports (no PyBullet needed)\n\n- Load shapes via &#96;read_obj_to_vertices&#96; (trimesh) -&gt; Shapely &#96;Polygon&#96; -&gt; &#96;GenericObject&#96; -&gt; &#96;ContactPointParameterization&#96;.  No PyBullet or simulation.\n- Standard path setup pattern from existing basic_test scripts (rospkg).\n- numpy, matplotlib for computation and plotting.\n\nKey existing code:\n\n- [&#96;src/legacy/object_utils.py&#96;](src/legacy/object_utils.py): &#96;GenericObject&#96;, &#96;ContactPointParameterization&#96; (methods &#96;parameter_to_point&#96;, &#96;get_contact_info&#96;, &#96;get_normal_vector&#96;), &#96;read_obj_to_vertices&#96;.\n- Shape OBJ files in &#96;urdf/&#96; directory: right_triangle, bolt, pi, root, rect, hourglass, meteor.\n\n## Section 1: Object Trajectory Propagation\n\n- Accept via argparse: shape name, &#96;t_param&#96; (contact point), body-frame velocity &#96;(vx_b, vy_b, omega)&#96;, duration, dt, initial pose.\n- Load shape: &#96;read_obj_to_vertices(obj_path)&#96; -&gt; &#96;Polygon(vertices)&#96; -&gt; &#96;GenericObject(polygon)&#96; -&gt; &#96;ContactPointParameterization(generic_obj)&#96;.\n- Get contact point in body frame relative to centroid:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;python\ncp_info = cpp.get_contact_info(t_param)\ncp_body = cp_info['point'] - np.array([centroid.x, centroid.y])\nn_out_body = cp_info['normal_outward']\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n- Euler propagation (no simulation, pure kinematics):\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;python\nfor each step:\n    R = rotation_matrix(theta)\n    pos += R @ v_body * dt\n    theta += omega * dt\n    # contact point in world\n    cp_world = pos + R @ cp_body\n    # contact point velocity in world\n    v_cp = R @ v_body + omega * R @ np.array([-cp_body[1], cp_body[0]])\n    # outward normal in world\n    n_out_world = R @ n_out_body\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n- Record: &#96;pos_history&#96;, &#96;cp_history&#96;, &#96;v_cp_history&#96;, &#96;n_out_history&#96;, &#96;theta_history&#96;.\n\n## Section 2: Holonomic Robot Matching\n\nThe robot is a circle of radius &#96;R_r&#96;. At each timestep, we place the robot center at:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nrobot_center = cp_world + R_r * n_out_world\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThe robot heading is &#96;zeta = atan2(cp_world - robot_center)&#96; (facing toward contact point), so the contact angle on the robot body is &#96;alpha = 0&#96; (front of robot). This is the natural choice, but we prove **any** alpha works:\n\nFor a holonomic robot with velocity &#96;(vx, vy, omega_r)&#96;, the contact point velocity is:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\nv_contact = [vx; vy] + omega_r * cross(k, r_base_to_cp)\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThis is 2 equations in 3 unknowns &#96;(vx, vy, omega_r)&#96; -- always underdetermined, so a solution always exists for **any** contact angle alpha.\n\nTo demonstrate: sweep alpha over &#96;[0, pi/4, pi/2, 3pi/4, pi]&#96; and show that each produces a valid &#96;(vx, vy, omega_r)&#96; matching &#96;v_cp&#96;. Plot the robot center trajectory and overlay the robot's contact-point trajectory (should be identical to the object's).\n\n## Section 3: Diff-Drive Robot Matching\n\nThe diff-drive robot has velocity &#96;(v_r, omega_r)&#96; with world-frame velocity &#96;[v_r cos(zeta); v_r sin(zeta)]&#96;. The velocity matching equation:\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n[v_cp_x]   [cos(zeta)   -R_r sin(zeta+alpha)] [v_r  ]\n[v_cp_y] = [sin(zeta)    R_r cos(zeta+alpha)] [omega_r]\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n**Determinant** = &#96;R_r * cos(alpha)&#96;. Non-zero whenever &#96;alpha != +/- pi/2&#96;, so a unique &#96;(v_r, omega_r)&#96; exists.\n\nAlgorithm (constant alpha, e.g. alpha=0):\n1. Initialize heading &#96;zeta_0&#96; (e.g., facing the object contact point from outside along normal).\n2. At each step, solve the 2x2 system for &#96;(v_r, omega_r)&#96;.\n3. Propagate heading: &#96;zeta += omega_r * dt&#96;.\n4. Robot center: &#96;cp_world - R_r * [cos(zeta+alpha); sin(zeta+alpha)]&#96;.\n5. Verify: robot's contact-point velocity == &#96;v_cp&#96; (should match by construction).\n\nRecord: &#96;robot_center_history&#96;, &#96;zeta_history&#96;, &#96;v_r_history&#96;, &#96;omega_r_history&#96;, and the robot-side contact point trajectory (should overlay object's).\n\n## Section 4: Plotting\n\n**Figure layout (2x3 or 3x2 grid):**\n\n1. **Object trajectory** (large/spanning subplot): shape outline at t=0 and t=T, CoM path (colored by time), contact-point path with quiver arrows for outward normal at sampled intervals.\n2. **Holonomic robot**: robot circles at sampled timesteps with heading arrow, robot center path, contact-point path overlaid on object's contact-point path. Optionally show multiple alpha values.\n3. **Diff-drive robot**: robot circles at sampled timesteps with heading arrow, robot center path, contact-point path overlaid on object's.\n4. **Velocity comparison** (time series): &#96;||v_cp||&#96; from object, from holonomic, from diff-drive -- should be identical.\n5. **Diff-drive internals** (time series): &#96;v_r(t)&#96;, &#96;omega_r(t)&#96;, &#96;zeta(t)&#96;, and the determinant &#96;R_r cos(alpha)&#96;.\n6. **Holonomic proof panel**: show solved &#96;(vx, vy, omega_r)&#96; for several alpha values, all producing the same contact velocity.\n\nSave to &#96;scripts/test/plots/&#96; or &#96;/tmp/&#96;.\n\n## Code Structure\n\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\ntest_matchingvelo.py\n    - parse_args()\n    - load_shape(name) -&gt; GenericObject, ContactPointParameterization\n    - propagate_object(v_body, omega, T, dt, x0, y0, theta0, cp_body, n_out_body)\n          -&gt; ObjectTrajectory dataclass\n    - holonomic_matching(obj_traj, robot_radius, alpha_values)\n          -&gt; HolonomicResult dataclass\n    - diffdrive_matching(obj_traj, robot_radius, alpha, zeta0)\n          -&gt; DiffDriveResult dataclass\n    - plot_results(obj_traj, holo_result, dd_result, shape_polygon, save_path)\n    - main()\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\n## Argparse defaults\n\n- &#96;--shape&#96;: \"pi\" (default), choices from OBJ file map + \"rect\"\n- &#96;--t_param&#96;: 0.25\n- &#96;--vx_body&#96;, &#96;--vy_body&#96;: 0.05, 0.0\n- &#96;--omega&#96;: 0.3 (gives an arc; set to 0 for straight line)\n- &#96;--duration&#96;: 5.0\n- &#96;--dt&#96;: 0.01\n- &#96;--robot_radius&#96;: 0.06\n- &#96;--alpha_dd&#96;: 0.0 (diff-drive contact angle on robot body)\n",

Good questions — let me address each.

## 1. Holonomic robot center: algebraic placement vs. propagation

You're right to flag this. In my code, I **algebraically place** the robot center at each timestep:

```python
center = cp_w + R_r * n_out
```

rather than propagating it from velocity. This is a shortcut. The argument for why it's equivalent:

- At time `t`, I compute the velocity `v_center(t) = v_cp - omega_r x r_base_to_cp` that the robot center **must** have.
- If the robot perfectly executes that velocity, then `center(t+dt) = center(t) + v_center(t) * dt` would land at (approximately) `cp_world(t+dt) + R_r * n_out_world(t+dt)`.
- The difference between algebraic placement and propagation is O(dt^2) — just Euler integration error.

So mathematically, the two approaches are equivalent in the continuous-time limit. But you're right that the code should ideally **propagate** the center from its velocity and then *verify* it stays at the correct offset — that would be a more honest demonstration. Right now I'm doing the "lazy but valid" version.

The same applies to the diff-drive case: I propagate the **heading** (`zeta += omega_r * dt`) but compute the center position algebraically. Again valid by the same argument — the velocity matching equation ensures positional consistency.

## 2. Diff-drive: determinant, existence, and smoothness

### Why determinant != 0 guarantees a solution

The velocity-matching equation is a standard 2x2 linear system:

```
A * [v_r; omega_r] = [v_cp_x; v_cp_y]
```

where:

```
A = [ cos(zeta)   -R_r sin(zeta+alpha) ]
    [ sin(zeta)    R_r cos(zeta+alpha)  ]
```

From linear algebra: a system `Ax = b` has a unique solution **if and only if** det(A) != 0, in which case `x = A^{-1} b`. When det(A) = 0, the two rows of A are linearly dependent — they point in the same direction — so certain `b` vectors can't be reached.

The determinant works out to:

```
det(A) = cos(zeta) * R_r cos(zeta+alpha) + R_r sin(zeta+alpha) * sin(zeta)
       = R_r * [cos(zeta) cos(zeta+alpha) + sin(zeta) sin(zeta+alpha)]
       = R_r * cos(zeta - (zeta+alpha))
       = R_r * cos(alpha)
```

The `zeta` cancels completely — the determinant depends **only on alpha** (the contact angle on the robot body) and the robot radius. So the heading of the robot doesn't matter for existence; only the contact angle does.

### Why alpha = +/-pi/2 is degenerate (geometric intuition)

When alpha = pi/2, the contact point is exactly **perpendicular to the heading** (on the robot's left or right side). Think about what the robot can produce at that point:

- **Forward velocity** `v_r` creates a velocity at the contact point along the heading direction (say, Y+).
- **Angular velocity** `omega_r` creates a velocity at the contact point tangent to the robot circle at that point — which, when the contact is on the side, is **also along the heading direction** (also Y+, or Y-).

Both `v_r` and `omega_r` produce velocities in the **same direction** at the contact point. They can't span 2D. So if the desired `v_cp` has any component perpendicular to the heading, it's unreachable.

When alpha = 0 (front contact), the forward velocity acts along the heading, while angular velocity acts perpendicular to it. They span 2D — any v_cp is reachable.

### The real issue: smoothness, not existence

This is your key observation and you're absolutely right. A solution existing (det != 0) says nothing about whether `(v_r, omega_r)` are reasonable or smooth. The closer alpha is to +/-pi/2, the closer det(A) is to zero, and by Cramer's rule the solution magnitudes blow up like `1/cos(alpha)`.

### Your rectangle example

Object (rectangle) moving in Y+, robot touches it on the right side. The contact point velocity is roughly in Y+. Consider the robot configurations:

**Config A: Robot faces toward the object (heading = pi, i.e., facing X-), alpha = 0 (front contact)**
- The robot's front touches the object's right side
- Forward velocity `v_r` pushes in X- direction
- `omega_r` must provide the Y+ component at the contact
- This works, but the robot is driving *sideways* relative to the motion — `omega_r` does all the heavy lifting, potentially large

**Config B: Robot faces Y+ (heading = pi/2), alpha ~ pi/3 (contact on front-left)**
- Forward velocity already goes in Y+, naturally matching the dominant velocity component
- `omega_r` provides the smaller correction
- Smoother, smaller control signals

**Config C: Robot faces Y- (heading = -pi/2), alpha ~ 0 (front contact), going backward (v_r < 0)**
- Robot reverses to track the Y+ motion
- Valid solution but `v_r < 0` — physically fine but unintuitive

So the **choice of alpha fundamentally changes the character of the solution** — it determines whether the robot goes forward or backward, whether control signals are smooth or wild, and whether the heading evolves slowly or rapidly. The existence proof (det != 0) just tells you a solution exists; it doesn't tell you it's a *good* one.

### What's really being chosen

You summed it up well: "technically, you can sum it up to be only the robot orientation that matter." That's almost right — it's really the **combination** of orientation `zeta` and contact angle `alpha` that determines the direction `phi = zeta + alpha` from which the robot approaches the contact point. Given a contact velocity `v_cp`, there are approach directions that align well with it (small, smooth controls) and ones that don't (large, oscillatory controls).

The deeper question — **how to choose (

Picking up where I left off:

### What's really being chosen (continued)

The deeper question — **how to choose (zeta, alpha) optimally** — is essentially: given the contact velocity `v_cp(t)` over time, find the approach direction `phi = zeta + alpha` that minimizes some cost on `(v_r, omega_r)`.

Since you have 2 equations and 4 unknowns `(zeta, alpha, v_r, omega_r)`, but `zeta` evolves dynamically via `zeta_dot = omega_r`, you really have **one free parameter at initialization** (the initial heading `zeta_0`, since alpha is held constant) plus the **one discrete design choice** of alpha.

A natural way to think about it: `phi = zeta + alpha` is the world-frame angle of the contact point on the robot. If you pick alpha so that phi roughly aligns with the **inward normal** of the object at the contact (i.e., the robot approaches from outside), then:

- The robot's forward axis is offset by alpha from that approach direction
- If alpha = 0, the robot drives straight toward/away from the contact — heading aligns with approach
- If alpha != 0, the robot drives at an angle to the approach direction

For your rectangle-going-Y+ example, the contact normal points in X- (into the object from the right). The approach direction phi should point in X+ (outward). So phi ~ 0. Then:

- If alpha = 0: heading zeta = phi = 0, robot faces X+. It needs to produce Y+ velocity at the contact using mostly `omega_r`. Awkward — heading is perpendicular to the motion.
- If alpha = -pi/4: heading zeta = pi/4, robot faces diagonally. Better split between `v_r` and `omega_r`.
- If alpha is chosen so that zeta ~ pi/2 (facing Y+): now `v_r` naturally produces Y+ motion, `omega_r` provides the small lateral correction. Smoothest solution.

So the **optimal alpha** is roughly the one that aligns the robot heading with the dominant direction of `v_cp`. But since `v_cp` and the approach direction can change over time (especially for arcs), there may not be a single alpha that's optimal throughout — which is exactly why this is a nontrivial design problem and worth testing numerically with different alpha values.

The current code fixes alpha as a constant and lets heading evolve. A more complete exploration would sweep over several alpha values and compare the resulting `(v_r, omega_r)` trajectories for smoothness — which would directly show your point about existence vs. quality.

If the robots are \emph{holonomic}, the problem is a velocity-tracking task: the velocity setpoint is obtained from a simple P-control comparing the current object state to the desired state, and can be realized using feedback such as motor encoders.
If the robots are \emph{non-holonomic} (e.g., differential drive), the desired contact-point velocity may not be feasible for a single robot; in that case, feasibility is addressed in the planning phase (e.g., by choosing waypoints and contact assignments so that the required contact velocities lie within the robot's motion constraints).

We can reduce the complexity of the robot-object dynamics by exploiting \emph{quasi-static}, also referred to as \emph{differential flatness} in this context \cite{pushing_revisited}.
When the object velocity is constant over a short time interval, the resulting trajectory is well-defined and admits a dual mapping between trajectory and velocity: the trajectory can be recovered from the flat output (e.g., the motion of a point related to the center of rotation), and vice versa.
For our object under AFC, such a segment is either a straight line or an arc \cite{pushing_revisited}.
The same observation holds for a differential-drive or Ackermann robot under constant velocity: the path is again composed of straight segments and arcs.
Therefore, if we represent the collision-free trajectory as a sequence of arcs and lines, there is a direct mapping from the object motion to the robot motion at each segment, provided the robot heading and the contact point on the robot are chosen appropriately.
This mapping is enforced at the velocity level by equating the object-side and robot-side contact velocities:
\begin{equation}
  \boldsymbol{v}_{\mathrm{contact}}
  \;=\;
  \zobjectvelocity
  \;+\;
  \zvelotheta \,\boldsymbol{k} \times \boldsymbol{r}_{\mathrm{com\text{-}to\text{-}contact}}
  \;=\;
  R(\zeta)
  \begin{bmatrix}
    v_r \\[2pt] 0
  \end{bmatrix}
  + \omega_r \times \boldsymbol{r}_{\mathrm{base\text{-}to\text{-}contact}},
\end{equation}
where the left-hand side reproduces \eqref{eq:background_velocity_at_point} and, for a differential-drive robot, $v_r$ and $\omega_r$ are the linear and angular velocities induced by the wheel speeds, mapped through the robot kinematics.

Concretely, this mapping amounts to finding two degrees of freedom per robot: the \emph{heading} $\zeta$ of the robot and the \emph{intended contact position} on the robot body, such that the contact-point velocity from the object side (given by \eqref{eq:background_velocity_at_point}) matches the contact-point velocity that the robot can produce at that body point.
A brief argument for existence: because the object pose has three degrees of freedom (position and orientation in $\zse$) while each robot contributes at least two (e.g., position of a point on the robot and its heading), the system is redundant; the mapping from the ``larger'' object motion to the ``smaller'' robot motion is underdetermined, so a solution that satisfies the contact velocity constraint can typically be found by suitable choice of robot heading and contact location.
This concludes our proposed method for configuration maintenance and object motion control.

Let me verify the math. The object contact velocity in world frame at time t is:

```
v_cp(t) = R(theta0 + omega_obj*t) @ v_cp_body
```

The robot contact velocity with constant (v_r, omega_r) is:

```
v_rc(t) = [v_r cos(zeta(t)), v_r sin(zeta(t))] + omega_r * [-R_r sin(phi(t)), R_r cos(phi(t))]
```

where `zeta(t) = zeta0 + omega_r*t` and `phi(t) = zeta(t) + alpha`. This factors as `R(omega_r * t) @ v_rc(0)`.

For all-time matching, we need: (1) `omega_r = omega_obj`, and (2) `v_rc(0) = v_cp(0)`. Condition (2) gives:

```
v_r cos(zeta0) = v_cp0_x + omega_obj * R_r * sin(phi0)   [call this 'a']
v_r sin(zeta0) = v_cp0_y - omega_obj * R_r * cos(phi0)   [call this 'b']
```

where `phi0` is fixed by the contact geometry (inward normal direction). This yields exactly **2 solutions**: `zeta0 = atan2(b,a)` with `v_r = +sqrt(a^2+b^2)` (forward), and `zeta0 + pi` with `v_r = -sqrt(...)` (backward).

1. **Problem statement** -- matching contact-point velocities between a circular robot and an object under constant body-frame velocity.

2. **Object kinematics** -- the key insight that the contact-point velocity in body frame is constant: `v_cp_body = v_body + omega x r_cp`. In world frame it simply rotates at rate omega.

3. **Contact geometry** -- how the approach direction phi, contact angle alpha, and robot center position are related.

4. **Holonomic robot** -- the underdetermined case (3 DOF, 2 constraints). The center position is algebraically determined at every instant; the center velocity in body frame is constant; omega_r = omega_obj. Zero tracking error by construction.

5. **Diff-drive robot** -- the fully determined case (2 DOF, 2 constraints). The derivation of the two conditions: (1) omega_r = omega_obj (both rotate at the same rate, preserving contact geometry), and (2) the initial velocity matching equation that yields exactly two solutions (forward and backward) with closed-form expressions for zeta_0, v_r, and alpha.

6. **Proof of all-time matching** -- factoring out the R(omega*t) rotation shows that t=0 matching implies all-time matching.

7. **Numerical verification** -- table of results from the test script across three scenarios.

8. **Planning implications** -- how this maps to the trajectory planning phase (decompose into arc/line segments, solve per-robot, check actuator limits).
